title: The Seventh Day
logline: On the seventh day after a death, a family cooks through the night, invites monks at dawn, and pours water until it overflows, saying a name out loud one more time.

object.note: Object 8 (identity not chosen) may appear subtly, for example among Chathura's things while he travels, waits or watches, only where it sits naturally in a real moment. Never staged, never the subject.

thread_in.thread: What is left behind leads to what the living still do: a family cooking through the night for a seventh-day almsgiving, pouring water until it overflows.

thread_out.thread: From a rite for someone gone to a night-long rite for someone still here: a village staying up with a family and a ritual specialist for a sick relative.

requirements: A family in the days following a bereavement who wants an almsgiving filmed
A neighbourhood temple with monks able to attend
Full, ongoing consent from every family member present

suggestions.name: A village in the Anuradhapura district
suggestions.why: A common setting for this practice with a nearby village temple; suggested for texture, not for a specific household.

unknowns: No participant, access or event has been found or confirmed.

lesson.in_simple_terms: The texts describe sharing a good deed with someone who has died as something done by telling: it is not enough to say 'share in this'. The living have to describe what they did well enough that the other could feel glad about it.
lesson.in_simple_terms_si: මියගිය කෙනෙකුට පින් දීමේදී 'මෙයින් කොටසක් ගන්න' කියා කීම පමණක් ප්‍රමාණවත් නොවන බවත්, කළ යහපත ඔවුන්ට සතුටු විය හැකි තරමට හොඳින් කියා පෙන්විය යුතු බවත් ග්‍රන්ථ කියයි.
lesson.the_teaching: Among the ten kinds of meritorious action, the Abhidhamma lists sharing merit (pattidāna) and rejoicing in merit shared by another (pattānumodanā). The Pradeepika says relatives who have died long to share in it, that the giver should recall wisely how the good deed was done while dedicating it, and that simply saying 'rejoice' without describing the deed makes it hard for a good state of mind to arise in the one who is meant to rejoice. The Margaya describes one class of unhappy being that lives on what others give in its name and waits for relatives to give it, and it limits this to that class rather than to everyone who has died.
lesson.how_the_film_shows_it: The film follows the work before the words: pots borrowed, a night of cooking, a front room rearranged, monks fed at dawn. When water is poured until it overflows and the family says the name aloud, the viewer sees remembrance happening as something the living do and say for someone else. The film never says where the person who died now is.

key_terms.en: rejoicing in merit shared by another
spirit that lives on what others give

lesson.caution: It does not mean the living are sending things to the dead, or that everyone who dies needs these offerings: in the texts the sharing works through gladness at a deed properly told, and dependence on offerings is said of one class of being only.
lesson.builds_on: The last film showed that a life ends unfinished and nothing of it travels on; this one shows what the living can still do, by telling the good they did in someone's name.
lesson.evidence_class: editorial interpretation grounded in cited source teaching
